paper_context.research_question: Can a transition-based parser with a novel transition set and neural feature representations accurately parse UCCA representations (DAGs with reentrancy, discontinuity and non-terminal nodes), and how does it compare to existing bilexical graph/tree and constituency parsers in-domain and out-of-domain?
main_claims: TUPA is the first parser for UCCA and supports the conjunction of reentrancy (multiple parents), discontinuous spans, and non-terminal nodes.
A transition set extended with NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE, SWAP and related constraints enables construction of general UCCA DAGs.
Using a BiLSTM-based feature extractor (TUPABiLSTM) substantially improves performance over sparse and MLP classifiers for UCCA parsing.

TUPABiLSTM outperforms a range of baseline bilexical graph parsers, constituency/discontinuous parsers, and tree-approximation approaches on both primary and remote edge F-scores, in-domain and out-of-domain.
The proposed parser attains primary-edge F-scores approaching reported inter-annotator agreement levels, indicating practical viability.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Labeled precision/recall/F1 on primary edges (how well core structure/predicate-argument relations are recovered)
Labeled precision/recall/F1 on remote edges (ability to recover reentrancy / multiple parents)
In-domain vs out-of-domain generalization (robustness across corpora)
Ablation or model-variant comparisons (sparse perceptron vs MLP vs BiLSTM)
Upper-bound analysis w.r.t. conversion to bilexical graphs/trees (loss from approximations)
Computational/implementation details (greedy inference, training stability, use of dynamic oracle)
Qualitative error analysis on discontinuities and non-terminal node prediction

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that (a) a newly designed transition system plus constraints can express UCCA foundational-layer graphs (DAGs with reentrancy, discontinuity and non-terminals); (b) implementing that system in a transition-based parser (TUPA) with neural classifiers, in particular a BiLSTM feature extractor (TUPABiLSTM), yields substantially better empirical performance on UCCA parsing than conversions to existing parser types and several baseline parsers; and (c) performance approaches inter-annotator agreement for primary edges, indicating practical viability. The chain of reasoning proceeds from formal system design (transition set and constraints), to classifier/feature design and training regime (dynamic oracle, greedy inference), to empirical evaluation (labeled-yield metric, comparisons to baselines via conversion, reporting primary and remote F-scores). Strengthening elements: explicit transition definitions, multiple classifier variants, in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation, and consideration of conversion upper bounds. Breaks/risks in reasoning: (1) theoretical completeness of the transition set is asserted but only deferred to an Appendix proof sketch — main text lacks formal proof or discussion of limits under greedy inference; (2) baseline comparisons rely on conversion procedures whose fidelity and heuristics are not exhaustively validated in the main text (Appendix D not shown here); (3) no variance/statistical significance reported for numeric gains; (4) key ablations (ratio feature, remote-children feature, role of pretrained embeddings, greedy vs beam) are not presented, weakening causal attribution of performance gains to specific design choices. Overall, the argument is coherent and mostly well-chained, but empirical claims would be better grounded by additional ablations, robustness checks, and clearer presentation of the completeness proof and dynamic oracle details.

prior_stage_inputs: SHARED_ANALYSIS_v1: extracted claims and assumptions; evaluation and reproduction targets; uncertainty flags
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces TUPA, a transition-based parser for UCCA (a foundational-layer semantic formalism) and a novel transition set intended to support three challenging properties jointly: reentrancy (remote edges), discontinuities, and non-terminal nodes. Three classifier variants are implemented (sparse perceptron, feedforward MLP, and BiLSTM + MLP). Training uses a dynamic oracle and greedy decoding. Evaluation employs a yields-and-labels matching metric, separating primary and remote edges, and compares TUPA variants to several baseline parsers by converting UCCA to bilexical graphs/trees (with reported conversion upper bounds). Main empirical finding: TUPABiLSTM substantially outperforms baselines on primary and especially remote edges in both in-domain (Wiki) and out-of-domain (20K Leagues) tests. The paper claims the transition set is complete (proof sketch in Appendix E) and that the approach achieves near-IAA primary F1. Key methodological foci for validation are: (1) theoretical completeness and operational realizability of the transition set under greedy decoding, (2) fidelity and correctness of conversion procedures (Appendix D) and reported upper bounds, (3) reproducibility of hyperparameters, dynamic oracle implementation and training schedules (Appendix C references), (4) robustness of empirical gains (variance, significance, multiple runs), and (5) ablation evidence isolating contributions of architecture vs features (ratio, remote-child count, pretrained embeddings, spaCy inputs).
logical_argument_graph: L1: UCCA requires parsing that supports reentrancy, discontinuity, non-terminal nodes -> existing parsers insufficient
L2: Transition-based parsing can be extended with new operations to produce UCCA graphs (NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE/REMOTE, SWAP, FINISH) -> design of TUPA transition set (Figure 2)
L3: The transition set is (claimed) theoretically complete for UCCA DAGs -> Appendix E proof sketch referenced
L4: Classifier choice impacts performance; BiLSTM feature extractor is hypothesized to improve prediction, especially for remote edges
L5: Train with dynamic oracle and greedy decoding -> learned policy approximates oracle behavior at test time
L6: Convert UCCA to bilexical graphs/trees for baseline training -> compute upper bounds for conversion loss
L7: Empirical results (Table 2) show TUPABiLSTM > baselines on primary and remote F1 -> supports claim that transition set + BiLSTM are effective
L8: TUPABiLSTM primary F1 approaches IAA -> claim of practical viability
L9: If any of A1-A10 (assumptions) fail, then L3-L8 can be invalidated or weakened (e.g., incomplete transitions, greedy decoding failures, conversion artefacts, lack of statistical robustness)

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript identifies a practical gap—no existing parser supports the conjunction of reentrancy, discontinuity and non-terminal nodes required by UCCA—and proposes an incremental, engineering-and-algorithmic contribution: a transition-based system (TUPA) with an extended set of transitions and constraints, a set of feature templates including two UCCA-specific features, and three classifier variants culminating in a BiLSTM-based feature extractor (TUPABiLSTM). The paper's argument proceeds as follows: (1) motivate transition-based methods from related parsing literature; (2) present a transition inventory designed to permit creation of non-terminals, remote edges (reentrancy), and discontinuous units (SWAP); (3) describe training with a dynamic oracle and three classifiers to probe the effect of model expressivity; (4) define a yields-based labeled evaluation metric separating primary vs remote edges; (5) compare TUPA to a set of baselines that are adapted by conversion to/from bilexical graphs or trees and report upper bounds on conversion loss; (6) present experiments in-domain and out-of-domain showing large gains for TUPABiLSTM, especially for remote edges. The paper positions the contribution as largely incremental: re-using transition-based parsing ideas and neural feature encoders but recombining and extending them to handle the specific representational conjunction that UCCA requires. The novelty claim is therefore twofold: (a) engineering/representation novelty in supporting the conjunction of three structural properties, and (b) empirical evidence that the particular transition set plus BiLSTM features produce stateful gains over converted baselines.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: UCCA requires DAGs with reentrancy, discontinuities and non-terminals; no single existing parser supports all three (Intro, Sec 2).
Solution design: Extend transition inventory with NODE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE_X, SWAP, plus SHIFT/REDUCE/FINISH and constraints to preserve validity (Sec 3, Fig 2).

Operationalization: Implement three classifier variants (sparse perceptron, feedforward MLP, BiLSTM+MLP) trained with a dynamic oracle and greedy inference; add UCCA-specific features including 'number of remote children' and a 'ratio' numeric regularizer (Sec 3).

Evaluation scaffold: Define yields-based labeled precision/recall/F1; separate primary vs remote edges; convert UCCA to bilexical graphs/trees to produce baselines and compute conversion upper bounds (Sec 4).
Empirical claim: TUPABiLSTM significantly outperforms baselines on primary and remote F1 in-domain and out-of-domain (Table 2, Sec 5).

Conclusion and implications: TUPA demonstrates that a grammarless transition-based parser with the proposed transitions and BiLSTM features can recover UCCA graphs at a level approaching IAA for primary edges, enabling broader use of UCCA in NLP tasks (Sec 7).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper identifies a concrete parsing gap—UCCA foundational-layer graphs require simultaneous support for reentrancy (remote edges), discontinuous units, and non-terminal nodes—and proposes a transition-based parser (TUPA) with a tailored transition set (including NODE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE_X, SWAP, FINISH) intended to be complete for UCCA DAGs. It implements three classifier variants (sparse perceptron, feedforward MLP, and BiLSTM feature extractor with MLP) trained with a dynamic oracle and greedy decoding; a set of UCCA-specific features (e.g., number of remote children) and a numeric 'ratio' regularizer are introduced to guide node creation. Empirically, TUPABiLSTM substantially outperforms converted-baseline bilexical graph/tree parsers on labeled primary and remote edge F1 in both in-domain and out-of-domain tests (Table 2), and the paper reports conversion-based upper bounds to contextualize baseline limitations. The authors argue that the transition set is theoretically sufficient (proof sketch in Appendix E) and that observed performance approaches practical limits (compared to reported IAA). The manuscript mixes theoretical design, engineering implementation, and empirical comparison; however, several methodological gaps (completeness proof accessibility, conversion fidelity, lack of variance/significance testing, missing ablations) temper how strongly the empirical claims support broad conclusions.
logical_argument_graph: A1: UCCA foundational-layer graphs require simultaneous support for reentrancy, discontinuity, and non-terminal nodes (problem statement).
A2: Existing parsers do not support this conjunction; hence a dedicated parser is necessary (motivation).
A3: Define an extended transition set (SHIFT, REDUCE, NODE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE_X, SWAP, FINISH) with constraints to permit constructing general UCCA DAGs (technical proposal).
A4: Implement TUPA with three classifier variants (sparse perceptron, MLP, BiLSTM) trained with a dynamic oracle and greedy decoding (engineering realization).
A5: Incorporate UCCA-specific features (number of remote children) and a ratio regularizer to control node creation (feature engineering).
A6: Evaluate using labeled-yield matching metric and compare to converted bilexical dependency/constituency baselines, reporting upper bounds for conversion loss (evaluation methodology).
A7: Empirical results: TUPABiLSTM outperforms other TUPA variants and baselines on primary and remote edges in-domain and out-of-domain (empirical claim).
A8: Conclude TUPA is effective for UCCA parsing and that the combination of transition design and BiLSTM features addresses the structural challenges (conclusion).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces TUPA, a transition-based parser designed to produce UCCA foundational-layer graphs, which require support for non-terminal nodes, reentrancy (remote edges), and discontinuous units. The authors define a transition inventory (SHIFT, REDUCE, NODE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE_X, SWAP, FINISH) with constraints, implement three classifier variants (sparse perceptron, MLP, BiLSTM+MLP) trained with a dynamic oracle under greedy decoding, and evaluate using a labeled-yield matching metric separating primary and remote edges. Empirically, TUPABiLSTM substantially outperforms converted bilexical graph/tree baselines on both primary and especially remote edge F1 in in-domain (Wiki) and out-of-domain (20K Leagues) tests. The paper claims (a) TUPA is the first UCCA parser that supports the conjunction of the targeted structural properties, (b) the transition set is complete for UCCA DAGs (proof sketch in Appendix E), (c) BiLSTM feature encoding yields major gains over sparse/MLP classifiers, and (d) performance approaches reported IAA for primary edges. These claims are largely supported by manuscript evidence (transition definitions, architecture descriptions, experimental numbers, conversion upper bounds), but several key aspects need verification or tempering: the completeness proof is only sketched/refereed to an appendix (not visible here), conversion fidelity and reconstruction heuristics determine baseline upper bounds and may bias comparisons, training/inference choices (greedy decoding, dynamic oracle specifics) and feature contributions (ratio, remote-child count, pretrained embeddings) lack isolating ablations and variance estimates. I therefore classify claims into supported, partially supported, and overstated categories below with evidence and uncertainty flags, and provide concrete actionable suggestions and alternative interpretations.
logical_argument_graph: Design goal: UCCA needs parser supporting non-terminals + reentrancy + discontinuities -> propose transition set enabling these operations (Section 3, Figure 2).
Operationalization: implement TUPA with stack, buffer, graph; define NODE and REMOTE edges to create non-terminal nodes and multiple parents; SWAP handles discontinuities (Section 3).
Learning: implement three classifiers (sparse perceptron, MLP, BiLSTM+MLP) trained with dynamic oracle; use greedy decoding (Section 3).
Features/regularizers: introduce UCCA-specific feature (number of remote children) and numeric 'ratio' regularizer; use pretrained word2vec and word dropout for NN models (Section 3).
Baselines: convert UCCA graphs to bilexical graphs/trees to train standard DAG/tree parsers; compute ‘upper bounds’ to quantify conversion loss (Section 4, Appendix D).
Evaluation: use labeled-yield matching metric; report separate primary and remote precision/recall/F1 (Section 4).
Empirical claim: TUPABiLSTM outperforms baselines on primary and remote F1 (Table 2) and approaches reported IAA on primary edges (Section 5).
Conclusion: transition set + BiLSTM encoder + dynamic training suffice to parse UCCA DAGs effectively; architecture has broader utility for DAG semantic parsing (Sections 5–7).

identified_claims.claim_text: Using a BiLSTM-based feature extractor (TUPABiLSTM) substantially improves performance over sparse and MLP classifiers for UCCA parsing.

Section 5 narrative: BiLSTM obtains substantially higher scores than other parsers and classifier variants.

identified_claims.claim_text: TUPABiLSTM outperforms a range of baseline bilexical graph parsers, constituency/discontinuous parsers, and tree-approximation approaches on both primary and remote edge F-scores, in-domain and out-of-domain.

Section 4: conversion procedures described and Appendix D referenced for details.

identified_claims.claim_text: The proposed parser attains primary-edge F-scores approaching reported inter-annotator agreement levels (73.5% vs IAA 80–85%), indicating practical viability.

The gap to IAA (6.5–11.5 points) remains nontrivial; claim that parser 'approaches' IAA is arguable but should be presented with caveats.

concerns.title: Completeness proof availability and assumptions
concerns.description: The paper asserts the transition set is complete for constructing UCCA DAGs but only references a proof sketch in Appendix E; the main text lacks formal proof detail and assumptions (e.g., node indexing, limits under greedy decoding).

concerns.title: Dependence on conversion fidelity for baseline comparisons
concerns.description: Comparisons to bilexical graph and tree baselines rely on conversion to/from UCCA and reported upper bounds; Appendix D governs this. If conversion heuristics lose information or reconstructions are imperfect, the baselines may be unfairly disadvantaged.

concerns.title: Lack of variance and statistical testing
concerns.description: Reported single-run F-scores lack confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; given remote-edge sparsity and stochastic training, observed improvements may not be robust across runs.
evidence: Table 2 reports point estimates only; prior-stage reviewers flagged missing variance and significance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run multiple (e.g., 5-10) random-seed replicates for key systems (TUPA variants and strongest baselines) and report mean±std and significance tests (e.g., paired bootstrap) for primary and remote F1.

concerns.description: BiLSTM-based model includes multiple changes (encoder, pretrained embeddings, word dropout, numeric ratio feature). The relative contribution of each is not quantified, limiting causal attribution for performance gains (particularly on remote edges).

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run targeted ablations: BiLSTM vs same MLP but with pretrained embeddings; with/without ratio feature; with/without number-of-remote-children feature; report remote and primary F1 deltas.

concerns.title: Greedy decoding may limit empirical realizability
concerns.description: Theoretical completeness does not guarantee greedy inference attains reachable gold graphs. Greedy decoding can cause irreversible errors (especially in node creation and remote edge attachment) that are not analyzed.
evidence: Section 3: authors state inference is greedy; assumptions in shared analysis note risk that greedy decoding may not produce some reachable graphs in practice.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate beam search (small beams) for TUPABiLSTM and report whether primary/remote F1 improves; analyze cases where greedy decoding prevents recovery (provide qualitative examples).

concerns.title: Dynamic oracle implementation and training details under-specified
concerns.description: Dynamic oracle behavior (tie-breaking, exploration policy, how random optimal transitions are sampled, and whether applied identically across perceptron and NN training) is summarized but not fully specified; this affects reproducibility and can influence which errors models learn to recover from.
evidence: Section 3: dynamic oracle described conceptually; Appendix C referenced for hyperparameters but not seen here.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers flagged missing tie-breaking and schedule details.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide precise dynamic oracle pseudocode, exploration schedule, and indicate differences in training for perceptron vs NNs; include random seed handling and number of epochs.

concerns.title: Evaluation metric limitations not fully discussed
concerns.description: The labeled-yield matching metric ignores order and internal structure beyond yields, which can mask errors in internal node organization or different analyses yielding same terminal sets; implications for non-terminal evaluation are not analyzed.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss metric limitations explicitly and provide complementary analyses: per-label confusion matrices, breakdown by constructions (discontinuities, coordination), and examples where different structures share yields but differ semantically.

If multiple runs with varied seeds show low variance and significance tests confirm gains, TUPABiLSTM's superiority is robust and the approach likely generalizes.

evidence: Figure 2 transition inventory extends standard transitions with REMOTE variants and NODE semantics; Section 3 ties to prior work (Sagae & Tsujii, Maier).
Empirical gains in Table 2 where TUPABiLSTM substantially outperforms modified baselines.
uncertainty_flags: Requires inspection of completeness proof and ablation to isolate which elements are novel vs reused.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Claimed support for the conjunction of three structural properties (non-terminals, reentrancy, discontinuity) is novel if both the transition set is theoretically complete and empirically realizable. Manuscript provides structured transitions and empirical evidence, but theoretical proof visibility and practical constraints (greedy decoding) must be validated.
evidence: Section 2 motivates the lack of parsers handling the conjunction; Section 3+Figure 2 propose an integrated transition set; Section 5 demonstrates empirical performance.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident in the empirical finding that TUPABiLSTM outperforms the evaluated baselines on the datasets and metrics shown, given the magnitude of reported gains and multiple corroborating descriptions. However, major methodological gaps (completeness proof accessibility, conversion fidelity, lack of variance/ablations) reduce certainty about the generality and causal attribution of the results, hence a conservative CI reflecting this mixed evidence.

consensus_findings: The manuscript addresses a genuine representational gap: UCCA foundational-layer graphs require handling the conjunction of non-terminals, reentrancy (remote edges), and discontinuities; the paper explicitly targets this gap.

A concrete transition inventory (SHIFT, REDUCE, NODE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE_X, SWAP, FINISH) is specified and operationalized in an implemented parser (TUPA) with clear transition semantics and constraints (Figure 2).

Three classifier variants are implemented (sparse perceptron, feedforward MLP, BiLSTM+MLP) and trained with a dynamic oracle under greedy decoding; the BiLSTM variant (TUPABiLSTM) attains substantially higher point-estimate scores than the other variants on reported test sets.

The experimental protocol includes in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation, distinguishes primary vs remote edges with an explicit labeled-yield matching metric, and reports conversion-based upper bounds for baseline adaptations.
TUPABiLSTM shows large empirical gains on remote-edge recovery compared to the converted baselines on the reported datasets and metrics.

Key reproducibility and validity dependencies are recognized by the authors and reviewers alike: (a) the completeness proof for the transition set is referenced (Appendix E) but not shown in the main text extract, (b) conversion/reconstruction procedures (Appendix D) underpin baseline comparisons and upper bounds, and (c) hyperparameters and oracle/ training details (Appendix C and training description) materially affect replicability.
disagreements: Extent of theoretical novelty: Some reviewers characterize the transition set as a meaningful representational novelty (combining three structural properties), while others view it as an incremental recombination of existing transition ideas (NODE, SWAP, graph transitions). Both positions were supported by citation comparisons and reasoning about prior work.

Degree to which empirical gains are attributable to the transition set versus the neural encoder and features: reviewers present controlled disagreement — several argue that BiLSTM contextual encoding and pretrained embeddings may drive much of the improvement, while others argue the REMOTE/NODE transitions are necessary to achieve remote-edge recovery. The reviewers agree this is unresolved without ablations.

Operational sufficiency under greedy decoding: reviewers differ on whether greedy inference is adequate in practice. Some see the reported results as evidence that greedy decoding works sufficiently; others caution that greedy decoding can prevent realizing theoretically reachable graphs and recommend beam/search comparisons.

Framing of novelty claim 'first parser for UCCA': reviewers recommend softer phrasing ('to our knowledge') and caution about asserting absolute primacy; some consider the claim plausible, others emphasize dependency on contemporaneous work verification.
uncertainty_hotspots: Completeness proof (Appendix E): reviewers flagged that the main theoretical sufficiency claim is deferred to an appendix proof sketch; correctness, formal assumptions, and constructive details must be inspected to validate theoretical claims.

Conversion/reconstruction fidelity (Appendix D): baseline comparisons and reported upper bounds depend on conversion heuristics; the magnitude and bias of conversion-induced information loss are uncertain and could materially affect relative results.

Attribution of empirical gains: the contributions of BiLSTM encoding, pretrained embeddings, spaCy-provided features, and UCCA-specific features (ratio, number-of-remote-children) are not isolated by ablation, creating uncertainty about which components drive performance.

Greedy decoding vs search: the interaction between greedy inference and the extended transition set (potential error propagation, unrealizable gold sequences) is an operational uncertainty that could alter empirical conclusions.
Statistical robustness: reported results are single point estimates without standard deviations or significance testing; particularly for sparse phenomena (remote edges), variance may be high.
Dynamic oracle implementation details: tie-breaking, exploration schedule and exact application across model variants are insufficiently specified, impacting reproducibility and training dynamics.
model_diversity_effects: Different reviewer roles emphasized different aspects: structure- and logic-focused reviewers highlighted the need for a formal completeness proof and precise transition semantics; methodology/auditing reviewers emphasized reproducibility artifacts (appendices, code, hyperparameters, baseline parity); novelty assessors focused on representational scope and whether the contribution is incremental or more disruptive.

This diversity surfaces complementary checks: structural reviewers pushed for theoretical validation (Appendix E), auditors demanded conversion diagnostics and multiple-run statistics, and novelty assessors requested ablations to separate representation vs encoder benefits. Together these perspectives identify concrete validation experiments and documentation needed to strengthen claims.

Role-specific emphases imply possible follow-up actions: theoretical reviewers favor formal lemmas/examples; empirical auditors favor reproducibility artifacts (code, commands, seeds, appendices); novelty assessors favor ablation tables and broader application cases.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Maintain a central decision role: request the authors to (1) include or make accessible the full completeness proof (Appendix E) with explicit assumptions and a concise constructive sketch in the main text, (2) provide full conversion/reconstruction pseudocode and diagnostics (Appendix D) including per-construction loss statistics and example failures, (3) report variance and statistical significance for key comparisons by running multiple random seeds (recommended >=5 runs) and applying bootstrap or paired tests for main pairwise contrasts (TUPABiLSTM vs strongest baselines) especially on primary and remote F1, (4) add targeted ablation studies isolating the contributions of BiLSTM encoding, pretrained embeddings (freeze vs update), UCCA-specific features (ratio, number-of-remote-children), and greedy vs small-beam decoding (beam sizes 2 and 5), (5) fully document the dynamic oracle implementation and training regimen (pseudocode, tie-breaking, exploration schedule), (6) supply exact commands, versions and configuration used for baseline systems to ensure parity, and (7) soften absolute 'first' claims to 'to our knowledge' unless authors can demonstrate contemporaneous literature search confirming absolute primacy. These items are requested for validation and not as acceptance criteria; the editor should weigh authors' responses and the additional materials before making further editorial determinations.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript's evidentiary base and reproducibility, provide the following: (1) completeness proof: include the full constructive proof or a clear, self-contained sketch that lists assumptions and addresses corner cases; add stepwise derivations for at least one complex UCCA graph requiring remotes and discontinuities, (2) conversion appendix: publish conversion and reconstruction algorithms with worked examples and per-construction loss statistics (how many non-terminals/remotes are irrecoverably lost), (3) ablations: run and report controlled ablation experiments isolating BiLSTM vs MLP, pretrained embeddings (freeze/update), presence/absence of 'ratio' and 'number-of-remote-children' features, and spaCy-derived features, (4) decoding experiments: evaluate greedy decoding vs small-beam search (e.g., beam 2 and 5) and report effects on primary and remote metrics, (5) robustness statistics: run multiple replicates (recommended >=5) with different seeds for core systems and report mean and standard deviation and perform statistical tests for main comparisons, (6) dynamic oracle details: supply pseudocode, sampling/tie-breaking policies and indicate precisely how perceptron and NN training use the oracle, (7) baseline parity: provide exact baseline command lines, versions, and preprocessing scripts so others can reproduce the comparative experiments, and (8) soften novelty wording where needed and add a short literature note if any near-contemporaneous work exists. Release code, trained models, oracle and conversion scripts publicly to enable independent verification.
transparency_report: Explicitly provided and visible in the manuscript: transition set table (Figure 2) with preconditions and effects; architecture descriptions for TUPA variants and TUPABiLSTM (Section 3, Figure 3); evaluation metric definition (labeled-yield matching) and separation of primary vs remote edges (Section 4); in-domain and out-of-domain experimental results (Table 2).

Deferred to appendices (referenced but not inspected in the provided extract): completeness proof (Appendix E), conversion and reconstruction procedures and heuristics (Appendix D), hyperparameters and training details (Appendix C). Reviewers flagged these as critical for verification.

Promised but not yet available in the review extract: public release of code, models, and scripts. Several reviewers noted that releasing oracle and conversion code is necessary for full reproducibility.

Undocumented or underspecified items in main text: exact dynamic oracle implementation details (tie-breaking, sampling schedule), per-run variance statistics, and conversion loss diagnostics. Baseline training/tuning commands and exact preprocessing pipelines were stated at a high level (e.g., spaCy used), but precise configurations were not included in the main text extract.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis is constrained by the provided materials and reviewers' access to the manuscript extract: (1) the completeness proof is only referenced (Appendix E) and was not available for independent inspection here, so claims about theoretical sufficiency remain partially unverified, (2) conversion procedures (Appendix D) were not inspected, so the degree to which baseline comparisons are affected by conversion-induced loss is uncertain, (3) empirical results are reported as single-run point estimates without variance, so robustness and statistical significance of reported differences cannot be established from available information, (4) dynamic oracle and training regimen specifics were not fully visible, limiting reproducibility assessment, and (5) data distribution details (counts of remote edges, per-construction frequencies) necessary to contextualize sparsity effects were not included in the extract. These limits mean the synthesized positions identify where evidence is present and where verification is required, but cannot definitively adjudicate causal attributions (transition set vs encoder vs features) or the absolute correctness of the theoretical completeness claim without the requested supplementary materials and replication artifacts.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes TUPA, a transition-based parser for UCCA that introduces an extended transition inventory (including NODE, LEFT/RIGHT-EDGE_X, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE_X, SWAP) intended to support non-terminal nodes, reentrancy (remote edges) and discontinuities. The authors implement three classifier variants (sparse perceptron, MLP, BiLSTM+MLP) trained with a dynamic oracle under greedy decoding, evaluate with a labeled-yield matching metric (separating primary and remote edges), and compare to multiple baselines via conversions to bilexical graphs/trees. Reported results show large point-estimate gains for the BiLSTM variant (TUPABiLSTM), particularly on remote edges, and the paper references appendices for a completeness proof of the transition set and for conversion/hyperparameter details.
strengths: Clear motivation: identifies a concrete representational gap (joint support for non-terminals, reentrancy, discontinuity) in existing parsers and aligns the technical design to that need.
Concrete transition inventory: Figure 2 and Section 3 specify transitions and operational constraints enabling inspectable implementation.

End-to-end systemization: implementation of three classifier families (sparse, MLP, BiLSTM) with a dynamic-oracle training regimen and practical engineering choices (DyNet, spaCy, pretrained embeddings).
Empirical breadth: in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations, separation of primary vs remote metrics, and reporting of conversion-based upper bounds for adapted baselines.
Promising empirical signal: large point-estimate improvements for TUPABiLSTM on both primary and especially remote F1 relative to converted baselines on the reported datasets.
limitations: Theoretical completeness claim deferred: the key claim that the transition set is complete for UCCA DAGs is referenced to Appendix E (proof sketch) but the main text lacks a self-contained theorem and assumptions; without inspecting the full appendix the theoretical sufficiency remains unverified.

Baseline-comparison dependence on conversion heuristics: comparative experiments rely on conversion/reconstruction procedures (Appendix D) that determine upper bounds; the fidelity and heuristics of these conversions are not documented in the main text, leaving potential bias in baseline performance unknown.

Lack of statistical robustness reporting: experimental results are presented as single point estimates without variance (multiple runs) or statistical testing, which undermines confidence in the stability of reported gains, particularly for sparse phenomena like remote edges.

Insufficient causal ablations and decoding analysis: the manuscript does not isolate contributions of core components (transition design vs BiLSTM encoder vs UCCA-specific features such as 'ratio' and 'number-of-remote-children'), nor does it evaluate greedy decoding vs beam search to quantify operational limits of greedy inference.
open_questions: Please provide (or point to) the exact constructive completeness proof (Appendix E): what formal assumptions are required, and how do node identity/indexing and SWAP/REDUCE interactions play into the constructive argument?

Provide conversion/reconstruction pseudocode and diagnostics (Appendix D): what fraction of gold non-terminals/remote edges are irrecoverably lost by conversion, and can you show representative failure cases?

How sensitive are the reported results to random initialization and training stochasticity? Please report mean ± standard deviation across multiple runs (recommended >=5) and perform statistical tests for the primary pairwise contrasts (TUPABiLSTM vs strongest baselines) for both primary and remote edges.

Please provide ablation experiments isolating: (a) BiLSTM vs MLP holding features constant, (b) with/without 'ratio' feature, (c) with/without 'number-of-remote-children' feature, and (d) freeze vs update pretrained embeddings; additionally, compare greedy decoding to small-beam search (e.g., beam=2,5).
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree the paper targets an important representational need for UCCA and provides an implemented transition-based parser with an explicit transition set and training pipeline.

There is broad agreement that the BiLSTM variant shows promising empirical performance on the datasets and metrics reported, with especially notable gains on remote-edge recovery in the provided point estimates.

Reviewers unanimously request inspection of appendices (full completeness proof, conversion details, hyperparameters) and additional empirical analyses (variance, ablations, decoding comparisons) to validate theoretical and empirical claims.
disagreement_snapshot: Some reviewers view the transition set as a meaningful representational novelty (supporting a conjunction of properties not jointly handled previously), whereas others view it as an engineering recombination of existing transition ideas (NODE, SWAP, graph transitions) and emphasize that empirical novelty may primarily come from the BiLSTM encoder.

Reviewers differ on whether greedy decoding is practically adequate: some regard the reported results as evidence greedy suffices, while others caution that greedy decoding can preclude realizing theoretically reachable graphs and recommend beam/search comparisons.

Degree of concern about conversion bias varies: some reviewers see reported conversion upper bounds as a careful mitigation, others consider conversion heuristics a critical unresolved confound that could substantially affect baseline competitiveness.
uncertainty_snapshot: Completeness-proof validity and its practical assumptions (Appendix E) are unknown from the provided materials; this is a major epistemic uncertainty.
Extent of conversion-induced bias in baseline comparisons (Appendix D) is uncertain: unknown how much of the observed margin is due to lost information vs model/regime differences.

Empirical robustness: absent multi-run statistics and significance testing, uncertainty about whether reported point estimates reflect stable improvements is substantial, especially for remote edges which are sparse.

Causal attribution: without ablations, uncertainty remains about whether gains stem mainly from the transition design, the BiLSTM encoder and pretrained embeddings, or the introduced UCCA-specific features.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper presents TUPA, a transition-based parser tailored to UCCA's foundational-layer graphs by adding NODE and REMOTE edge transitions and SWAP to handle discontinuities. It implements three classifier regimes and reports that the BiLSTM variant substantially improves primary and remote edge recovery versus converted baselines, with conversion upper bounds provided.
Strengths: The work identifies a concrete representational gap, supplies a clear transition inventory that maps to UCCA phenomena, provides an implemented system and multiple classifier variants, evaluates both in-domain and out-of-domain, and reports large point-estimate gains (notably on remote edges).
Limitations: (1) The central theoretical claim (transition-set completeness) is only referenced to an appendix proof sketch (Appendix E); the main text lacks a clear formal statement and assumptions—inspect the appendix and include a concise theorem/constructive sketch in the main text. (2) Baseline comparisons depend on conversion/reconstruction heuristics (Appendix D) that determine upper bounds; the main text lacks conversion pseudocode and diagnostics quantifying information loss, so baseline performance may be biased. (3) Results are single-run point estimates without reported variance or statistical testing, which weakens claims about robustness, especially for sparse remote edges. (4) The manuscript lacks targeted ablation studies isolating feature and encoder contributions and does not analyze greedy decoding vs beam search; causal attribution to the transition set vs BiLSTM/feature engineering is thus unresolved.
Open Questions: (1) Please supply the complete constructive completeness proof and state its assumptions: can you show a derivation example for a complex UCCA graph involving multiple remotes and discontinuities? (2) Provide the conversion/reconstruction algorithms and quantitative diagnostics: what percentages of non-terminals and remote edges are unrecoverable by conversion? (3) Share multi-run statistics and significance tests for key contrasts (recommended >=5 runs); how stable are remote-edge F1 results? (4) Provide ablation results that separate the impact of BiLSTM vs MLP, pretrained-embedding policies (freeze/update), the 'ratio' and remote-child features, and greedy vs beam decoding.
Transparency: The paper provides the transition inventory, model architectures, evaluation metric and point-estimate results in the main text. However, critical reproducibility materials (full completeness proof, conversion/reconstruction algorithms, hyperparameters and dynamic oracle specifics) are deferred to appendices and not available in the extract; reviewers requested these appendices and the release of code/models (including oracle and conversion scripts) to validate claims.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects substantial evidence of a working system with promising point-estimate gains (especially for remotes) and clear engineering/representation work, tempered by major verification gaps: the completeness proof is only sketched in appendices, conversion procedures underpin baseline comparisons, no multi-run statistics or ablations were provided, and dynamic-oracle/decoding behaviors are underspecified. If authors supply appendices, code and requested experiments, confidence in the claims should increase materially.
